slides.title: A Roth IRA at 16? Here's how
slides.sub: If you earn money from work, you can open a Roth IRA at any age.

slides.heading: What a Roth IRA is
body: A Roth IRA is a retirement account. You put in money you've already paid tax on, so your contributions aren't deductible.
The payoff: qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free, including all the growth.

slides.heading: Who can open one
body: You can contribute at any age if you have taxable compensation, like pay from a job. Under 18? A parent usually opens it as a custodial account.
The 2026 limit is $7,500, or what you earned that year if it's less.

slides.heading: Why start at 16
body: Example: put in $2,000 a year at ages 16, 17 and 18, then stop. If it grows 7% a year (an assumption, not a promise), that's about $154,600 at 65.
Only $6,000 is your money. The rest is growth, and in a Roth, qualified withdrawals of it are tax-free.
slides.source: HFLIC calculation; returns are not guaranteed

slides.takeaway: Earned money this year? Ask a parent about opening a custodial Roth IRA.

posts.caption:
Have a job? You can open a Roth IRA at any age, as long as you have taxable compensation like pay from work (IRS). If you're under 18, a parent usually opens it as a custodial account.

How it works: you put in money you've already paid tax on, and qualified withdrawals in retirement come out tax-free, growth included. The 2026 limit is $7,500, or what you earned that year if it's less.

Example: $2,000 a year at ages 16, 17 and 18, then nothing else. At an assumed 7% a year, that $6,000 grows to about $154,600 by 65. The 7% is an assumption, not a promise, but time is on your side.

Data: IRS (Traditional and Roth IRAs; Topic 309); 2026 limit from IRS Notice 2025-67 via CPA Practice Advisor.
